title: Connectome analysis of a cerebellum-like circuit for sensory prediction.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Zenodo record 19892261 via API: CC-BY-4.0, two files, EM_data_published.zip (7,401,502,090 bytes) and efish_em_ELL-main.zip (969 KB code). Downloaded and read the code zip: README lists the archive contents (df_type_auto_typed.csv, df_postsyn.csv, df_presyn.csv, morphology_cat/, reconstructions_published/ JSON files). Notebook outputs show 5,025 reconstruction files; CellTyping.ipynb shows the final cell-type labels were adjusted by hierarchical clustering and logistic regression on morphology features (mg 104 / sg 545 cells in the cluster step; sg1 388 / sg2 171). Zenodo ignored an HTTP Range request (returned 200 with the full 7.4 GB body), so the CSVs inside the zip could not be opened. Listed the public Google Cloud bucket efish-public: EM image and segmentation volumes in neuroglancer format plus neuroglancer state JSONs.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: About 10,000 cell bodies in the volume, about 5,000 reconstructed, about 3,000 sorted into 8 cell types, and about 30,000 manually annotated synapses: these figures come from the project landing page and abstract. I never saw the row counts of the cell-type or synapse tables. The Nature full text is paywalled; I did not read the bioRxiv/PMC preprint text.

a1_downloadable.note: Public Zenodo record, CC-BY-4.0, no login needed. But the small tables sit inside a single 7.4 GB zip with no ranged access, so I couldn't open them here (over the 50 MB cap).

a2_label_is_a_column.note: From the notebook code (not the file itself), df_type_auto_typed.csv has a 'cell_type' column keyed by cell 'id', and df_postsyn.csv has pre/post/structure/x/y/z per synapse. Not opened.

a3_inputs_present.note: Connectivity (synapse edge lists) and morphology summaries are said to be in the archive as CSVs, per the README and notebooks. Not opened.

a4_units_stated.note: Voxel size 16×16×30 nm is stated in the code. Coordinate units in the CSVs are in voxels or nm depending on the column, according to the notebooks. Not verified in the files.

a5_enough_rows.note: About 3,000 typed cells across 8 types (landing page), which clears the 400-row classification bar. Subtype sets are small (sg1 388 / sg2 171, mg 104 in notebook outputs). I never saw the exact typed-cell count.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: Under 1 GB of CSV/JSON after extraction (estimate); needs a 7.4 GB one-time download
a6_fits_laptop.note: The tables are small, but you have to download the whole 7.4 GB zip to get them. No GPU needed for a graph or tabular baseline.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The 5,025 reconstruction files in the notebook output match the landing page's 'about 5,000 reconstructed'. I couldn't check the typed-cell or synapse counts in the files.

a8_label_provenance.note: Cell types are manual expert calls, refined by clustering and logistic regression on morphology features (seen in CellTyping.ipynb). Predicting type from morphology would therefore be circular. Predicting it from connectivity only is not. Passes only under that restriction.

B1.why: Cell-type table plus synapse edge lists joined on cell id (per README); not opened.

B2.why: CSVs per README, untested; reaching them needs a 7.4 GB zip extraction.

B3.why: Single volume, single team's typing scheme; labels are internally consistent by construction.

B4.why: Categorical labels, no censored values expected; unverified.

B5.why: Cells cut by volume edge ('ov' out-of-volume flag in notebook) give partial reconstructions; need filtering.

B6.why: Archive ships a CONTENTS.md per README; notebooks explain columns partially. Not seen.

C1.why: Whether wiring alone recovers ELL types is informative either way, but a niche question.

C2.why: Connectivity-based cell typing is established on FlyWire; nothing found on this fish data.

C3.why: Diversity angle: first teleost cerebellum-like connectome; weak given single animal.

C4.why: Expert cell typing in EM is manual and slow, but ~3,000 cells already typed here.

C5.why: Majority class and authors' morphology clustering are obvious dummies; no published connectivity-typing number.

D1.why: No open-weight pretrained backbone for small connectivity graphs; SegCLR-style image embeddings need full EM volume.

D2.why: No freeze-and-head route; would train a graph model or gradient boosting from scratch.

E1.why: Spatial block split across the 450 µm volume using soma coordinates (in reconstructions, per code).

E2.why: Volume can be cut into ≥5 spatial blocks; class balance per block unknown.

E3.why: Majority class and per-layer soma-depth rule are computable.

E4.why: No repeated independent typing of the same cells to estimate label noise.

E5.why: Known: MG cells inhibit Output cells; granule cells feed MG apical dendrites (paper's main finding).

E6.why: Label shuffle and degree-preserving edge rewiring are runnable.

E7.why: No second ELL connectome; single fish, single volume.

E8.why: Authors report no cell-type classification accuracy to reproduce.

G1.why: Cell ids are segment ids internal to this volume; no standard cross-dataset identifier.

G2.why: Mouse cerebellum or fly mushroom body connectomes plausible comparators, but no shared key.

G3.why: No join exists; cross-species comparison would be by analogy, not by key.

G4.why: Cross-species 'are cerebellum-like wiring motifs conserved' is interesting but not a join.

H1.why: Absent synapses are informative only within fully reconstructed cells; most cells partial.

H2.why: One fish, one 450×450×105 µm volume, one lab.

H3.why: Claim stated precisely below, restricted to this volume and connectivity-only features.

H4.why: Volume-edge truncation flagged in code ('ov'); sparse reconstruction bias less explicit.

I1.why: Sawtell lab and connectomics cell-typing community; no stated demand for automation here.

I2.why: Could speed typing of the ~5,000 untyped bodies in the volume; marginal.

I3.why: Balanced accuracy matches a typing aid roughly; no defined decision threshold.

I4.why: Authors typed SG/MG with a 2-feature logistic regression; major types may be rule-separable.

J1.why: Graph ML on a small connectome, but no pretrained transfer component.

J2.why: Paper gives clear connectivity rules to sanity-check against; needs neuroscience intuition.

J3.why: Cleaned edge list plus typing baseline is shareable; impact limited.

existing_models.name: FlyWire connectivity-based cell typing (Schlegel et al. / Dorkenwald et al., Nature 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Fly cell types can be predicted by a logical conjunction of on average five synaptic-partner types (from search summary; exact accuracy and split not retrieved).

existing_models.name: fly-connectome (GitHub, kostas52675): cell-type prediction from FlyWire connectivity

backbone.name: none suitable; gradient boosting or a small graph neural network trained from scratch

integration.partner_dataset: FlyWire (fly) or MICrONS (mouse) connectomes, compared by analogy only
integration.join_key: none (no shared identifier; cross-species comparison of motif statistics)
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Are the wiring rules that define cell types in cerebellum-like circuits shared between fish and fly mushroom body?

controls.positive_control: The model must recover that Output cells receive MG-cell inhibitory input and that granule cells contact MG apical dendrites (paper's described connectivity).
controls.negative_control: Label shuffle; degree-preserving rewiring of the synapse graph should drop accuracy to the soma-depth baseline.
controls.external_validation: None: no second ELL connectome exists.

honest_claim_h3: Within one 450×450×105 µm EM volume from one Gnathonemus petersii, synaptic partners and target compartments alone predict the expert-assigned cell types of reconstructed ELL (electrosensory lobe) neurons, with accuracy measured on spatially held-out blocks.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use only who each neuron connects to, and where, to predict its expert-assigned cell type in an electric-fish brain circuit.
plain_idea.train_on: For each reconstructed neuron, counts of incoming and outgoing synapses by partner type and by target compartment (axon, apical or basal dendrite, soma). About 3,000 typed cells according to the landing page; I didn't verify the exact count.
plain_idea.predict: The cell type (8 classes, e.g. MG, Output, granule cell), assigned by the authors from morphology, partly refined with clustering and logistic regression on shape features.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: This would show whether wiring alone defines cell types in a vertebrate cerebellum-like circuit, as it does in the fly. It could also help type the ~5,000 still-unclassified bodies in this volume.

more_or_better_data.why: Much smaller than FlyWire (139,255 neurons). Its edge is diversity: it's the only teleost cerebellum-like connectome found, a circuit type none of the existing models were built on.

confidence_score.why: There's no repeated typing of the same cells and no second animal, so per-prediction uncertainty can't be calibrated against label noise.

models_beatable.why: The FlyWire typing methods are rule-based and species-specific, and they can't run on this data. There's no published model on this data to beat.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No existing model can be run as a baseline on this data, and there is no new data that joins to it on the same quantity.

label_elsewhere.sources: Connectome cell-type annotations exist at scale in FlyWire (known resource) and MICrONS (known resource), but for other species and circuits with different type vocabularies.
label_elsewhere.join_key: none; type vocabularies differ across species
label_elsewhere.why: Other connectomes allow only analogy-level transfer tests (e.g. cerebellum-like motif statistics), not extra labelled ELL cells.

risks: The cell-type labels were partly assigned by clustering and logistic regression on morphology features, so any morphology or soma-depth feature leaks the label.
Neighbouring cells share synaptic partners, so a random split leaks local wiring between train and test.
Partner-type features use the labels of other cells, so test-cell labels can leak in through their partners' features.
Cells cut by the volume edge have truncated connectivity that correlates with layer, and so with type.
leakage_plan.split: Hold out spatial blocks of the volume, built from soma x/z coordinates in the reconstruction JSONs (not seen in files). Compute partner-type features using training-set labels only.
checks: Shuffle the labels and confirm accuracy falls to majority class.
Train on soma depth alone to measure how much is layer position rather than wiring.
Compare random-split accuracy with spatial-block accuracy; a big gap means local leakage.
leakage_plan.verdict: Manageable if morphology features are excluded and partner labels are masked, but leakage through partner labels is subtle.

success_criteria.metric: Balanced accuracy across the 8 cell types on spatially held-out blocks, because the use case is typing every class, including rare ones.
success_criteria.baselines: Majority class, and a soma-depth-only classifier (both computable, numbers unknown). No published number exists.
success_criteria.success: Connectivity-only balanced accuracy at least 0.15 above the soma-depth-only baseline on held-out blocks (threshold chosen by me, not from a source).
success_criteria.kill: If, after the 7.4 GB download, fewer than 1,500 cells have both a type label and at least 10 annotated synapses, or connectivity adds under 0.05 over soma depth, stop.

ambitious.why: Publishes circuit neuroscience with computational analysis. It would need wiring-defined types that generalise to the untyped bodies and match the physiology.

realistic.why: Publishes analysis notes on public connectomes. A careful connectivity-versus-morphology typing comparison on this volume fits.

fallback.journal: bioRxiv preprint plus a NeurIPS/ICLR connectomics or graph-learning workshop
fallback.why: Even a negative result (wiring adds nothing beyond layer depth) is a short workshop note.

pitch.headline: A public, CC-BY electric-fish connectome: about 5,000 reconstructed neurons, about 30,000 hand-annotated synapses, and no ML work on it found.
pitch.what_makes_the_data_unusual: The only teleost cerebellum-like circuit connectome found. Synapses were annotated by hand, not predicted, which the landing page states. 5,025 reconstruction files confirmed in the notebook output. Counts of typed cells and synapses come from the paper only.
pitch.the_win: Connectivity-only typing that beats soma-depth position by at least 0.15 balanced accuracy on held-out spatial blocks.
pitch.even_if_it_fails: We'd learn that ELL cell types are mostly set by layer position rather than wiring partners. That is a modest note, not a paper.
pitch.who_wants_it: The Sawtell lab (Columbia) and Lichtman/Google connectomics groups, for typing the ~5,000 unclassified bodies still in this volume.

ml_idea: Build per-cell features from df_postsyn/df_presyn (partner-type and compartment counts, with partner labels masked to the training set) and classify the 8 ELL cell types with gradient boosting or a small graph neural network. Evaluate on spatial blocks, against a soma-depth baseline.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed. The tables are small (thousands of cells, about 30,000 synapses), but you need a one-time 7.4 GB download and extraction to reach them.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Download the zip, then count rows in df_type_auto_typed.csv by cell_type and the cells with at least 10 synapses in df_postsyn.csv. If fewer than 1,500 qualify, stop.

verdict_reason: The data is public (CC-BY), but the tables sit inside a single 7.4 GB zip I couldn't open. It's one fish, one volume, with no pretrained backbone and no external validation. The cell-type labels were partly assigned by morphology clustering, so only connectivity features are legitimate. Modest value for the effort.
